fixes.explanation: Yes, the Herodians. The text says the Pharisees sent their disciples to Him "…along with the Herodians." So the question comes from that group, not from the Pharisees themselves. Sending a whole delegation to ask one question is a plan with a lot of moving parts.
Not the Samaritans. Matthew 22:16 says the Pharisees sent their disciples to Him "…along with the Herodians." The Samaritans aren't named in that verse. The Herodians are the answer here, friend.

Not the Levites. The text says the Pharisees sent their disciples "…along with the Herodians." The Levites aren't named in this verse. Look at who goes with the disciples, and you'll find the Herodians.

Right, because the text says the opposite. They tell Jesus, "You seek favor from no one, because You pay no attention to external appearance." That's another compliment on the pile. They keep stacking them higher and higher, like cookies on one plate.

Yes, taxes. They ask, "Is it lawful to pay taxes to Caesar or not?" The text says the Pharisees conspired to trap Jesus in His words (Matthew 22:15). So this yes-or-no question comes straight out of that plan. Keep that in mind as the story goes on, baker.
That's not the word they use. They ask, "Is it lawful to pay taxes to Caesar or not?" The word in the verse is taxes. It's a close guess, but tithes isn't what they say.
Not wages, though I'd love a question about my wages sometime. They ask, "Is it lawful to pay taxes to Caesar or not?" The word is taxes. Wages never come up in their question.

Yes, the same men who came to test Him. Jesus says, "Show Me the coin used for the tax." and the text says, "…they brought Him a denarius." So the men testing Him are the ones who bring the coin. I think it's funny that their test brings its own coin, but that's just me.

Simon Peter, one of Jesus' twelve disciples (Matthew 10:2), isn't named in this passage. The text says "…they brought Him a denarius." That "they" is the ones who came to Him with the question in verse 16. Good guess on a name you know, though.

Caesar's! Jesus asks, "Whose image is this, and whose inscription?" and they answer, "Caesar’s." Notice that Jesus is the one asking now, and they're the ones answering. I think that's a nice switch. Their own answer sets up what Jesus says next.

Herod isn't the name they give. Asked whose image and inscription are on the coin, they answer, "Caesar’s." It's the same Caesar from the tax question. Then Jesus talks about Caesar and God, not Herod.

Right. What Jesus actually says is, "Give to Caesar what is Caesar’s, and to God what is God’s." He never tells them not to pay. He answers the question with the coin they brought Him, and with one line about Caesar and God.
Yes. The text says, "…when they heard this, they were amazed." Then they left Him and went away. They came to trap Him in His words, and they walked away amazed instead. I'd be amazed too, baker.

Nope, they were amazed. The text says, "…when they heard this, they were amazed." After that, they left Him and went away. The men who came to trap Him in His words ended up standing there amazed, and I think that's quite a turnaround, friend.
